did_you_know.text: Did you know? Jeremiah was commanded to stand specifically at the gate of the Lord’s house, where worshipers entered, and deliver his warning there to all Judah.
Did you know? The people repeated the slogan “The temple of the Lord” three times, but Jeremiah warned them not to regard the mere existence of the temple as a guarantee of security.

Did you know? Alongside faith in the Lord, the prophet also demands social responsibility: administering justice, protecting the foreigner, the orphan, and the widow, and refraining from shedding innocent blood.
Did you know? Jeremiah calls the temple a “den of robbers” when people use it as a supposed refuge while continuing to commit injustice.

Did you know? In his speech, Shiloh serves as a historical example of a place where the Lord’s name once dwelt but was destroyed because of Israel’s wickedness; in this way, the prophet warns that the temple is not immune from destruction either.
Did you know? In this chapter, Jeremiah is commanded not to pray for the people, not to cry out or pray on their behalf, and not to plead with the Lord for mercy for them.
Did you know? Idolatry is described as a family activity: the children gather wood, the fathers kindle the fire, and the women knead dough to prepare “cakes” for the Queen of Heaven.
Did you know? Jeremiah emphasizes that the central command given to Israel at the time of the Exodus was to obey the Lord’s voice and be his people; sacrifices alone are no substitute for obedience.

Did you know? At Topheth, in the Valley of Ben-Hinnom, rituals were performed that involved burning sons and daughters in the fire or making them pass through the fire; the prophet emphasizes that the Lord never commanded such acts.

Did you know? Following the destruction, Topheth and the Valley of Ben-Hinnom will be called the “Valley of Slaughter,” because the place will be filled with graves until there is no room left for burial.
